title: The Devil Is in the Details
author: FiveTwelveThirteen
summary: FiveTwelveThirteen argues that the gap between a good educational idea and its successful classroom implementation is almost entirely located in the unglamorous details that leaders and teachers tend to skip or underestimate. The article diagnoses a persistent pattern in schools: a compelling framework is adopted, communicated to staff, and then fails to produce results — not because the idea was wrong, but because the implementation decisions (sequencing, pacing, modelling, scaffolding, feedback loops) were never properly specified. Drawing on examples from direct instruction, retrieval practice, and formative assessment, the piece shows how each approach degenerates into a weak caricature when the procedural details are left vague. The author makes a case for detail-rich implementation planning: anticipating failure points, scripting difficult moments, and building concrete monitoring mechanisms that go beyond lesson observation. The piece concludes that the most important leadership question is not whether an initiative was launched but whether it was specified precisely enough for anyone to know what success actually looks like.
points: The implementation gap is a detail gap: most failed school initiatives are undone not by wrong ideas but by vague execution plans that leave too many decisions to individual interpretation or professional chance.

Effective implementation requires detail-rich planning — identifying every failure point in advance, specifying the exact behaviors expected at each stage, and naming concretely what 'done well' looks like.

Approaches like retrieval practice and formative assessment degrade rapidly into rituals without substance when implementation details are absent: the technique is present in classrooms but the mechanism that produces learning is not.

Leaders who treat implementation as a communication problem rather than a design problem consistently underestimate the number of explicit decisions required — and consistently overpay in re-launches for under-specified original rollouts.

Monitoring must be built into implementation from the start: what gets measured, when, and by whom determines what actually changes in classrooms, and monitoring added after the fact almost never catches the same problems early monitoring would prevent.
quotes: I’ve ended up in a few conversations online recently about teaching that make me want to give a really specific example of how I teach something. Conversations about teaching are hard because lots of stuff sounds good in the abstract, but in real teaching the devil is in the details.
Let’s get specific. One topic I teach is multiplying negative numbers. Here’s how I approach that topic.
Here I step in. I leave those last few problems on the board, and I say hey, when we say 2 x (-3), what we mean is -3 + (-3), so 2 x (-3) is -6.
I’ll give a few more examples, this time juxtaposing multiplying positives and negatives. What is 2 x (4)? Ok, what is 2 x (-4)?

Then I step in. 10 x (-6) is -60, so -6 x 10 is also -60. Again, I give a few more examples, check for understanding, and we practice a bit, again with some mixed practice. I do something similar for a negative times a negative, activating prior knowledge and looking at patterns to help students see why a negative times a negative makes a positive.
This might have to do with my context. My school has persistently low math achievement. I teach a lot of students who, for years, have felt unsuccessful in math class.
